newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels say clash with army left casualties.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels say clash with army left casualties.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas said their forces clashed recently with the Mexican army and they predicted more fighting as the government steps up efforts to hunt them.
Interior Ministry officials were not available for comment on the rebel claim.

In a statement obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) said there had been several casualties on both sides due to clashes between the army and rebel units. The group did not give specific dates.

"The persecution of our military units by the bad government's armed forces is more frequent each day and uses a larger number of troops, a situation that has led to several clashes, resulting in casualties on both sides," the EPR said.
The EPR, believed to number several hundred well-armed fighters, first appeared in June 1996 calling for the overthrow of the government and the establishment of a Marxist workers' state.
It carried out a wave of attacks at the end of August 1996 but has since confined itself mainly to propaganda actions.
In the statement the EPR accused the government of carrying out a brutal counter-insurgency campaign, sweeping villages in search of the elusive guerrillas and torturing suspected members.
"Several villagers in these areas have been detained and tortured to get them to finger EPR members," the EPR said.

"Given the harassment our military units are facing in different parts of the country, clashes with the federal army and police are imminent and could take place at any time, so that our troops can repel the aggression," the group added.

The rebels said army troops backed by helicopters and light artillery combed large areas of several states, while police and paramilitary groups used strong-arm tactics to find rebel sympathisers in local villages.
"In sweeping these areas, villages and their residents are subject to threats, intimidation, repression, humiliation, arrogance and searches of their homes," the statement said.
Although the EPR claims its numbers have been growing, the group poses no serious military threat to the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.
Scores of EPR suspects have been arrested since the group appeared, although few have been formally charged.
Left-wing groups claimed that dozens of innocent activists were being unjustly held on charges of helping the EPR but the government denied this.
